You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Diagnosis:
The bug report mentions that a TAR archive with a checksum padded with zeros on the left (right-aligned) causes a checksum failure. The TAR specification expects the checksum field to be terminated by a NULL or SPACE character on the right, but the linked TAR file violates this by zero-padding on the left. This results in the last two digits of the checksum being lost and causes validation to fail.

Inspecting the method `TarUtils.verifyCheckSum(byte[])` reveals that it verifies the checksum by reading up to 6 octal digits in the checksum field, starting from the beginning of the checksum area and only counting digits up to 6. It then computes the sum of the bytes in the header (with the checksum field replaced by spaces) as an unsigned and signed sum. It returns true if the stored checksum matches either sum.

The method parses the checksum digits in a strict manner: any digit after 6 is not counted, and non-octal characters cause ending of the digit count. The TAR linked in the bug report apparently contains a checksum where digits are right-aligned with zero-padding on the left instead of using the expected scheme. Hence, only the first 6 octal digits are considered, potentially truncating the checksum and omitting the last two digits.

The existing code also replaces the checksum bytes with a space (ASCII 32) for the purpose of checksum calculation. This matches the specification, which expects spaces or NULLs on the right side of the checksum. This means the code is not built to handle trailing zeros on the left side of the checksum, which the bad archive uses.

Hence, the root cause is the inflexible logic in `verifyCheckSum` that looks only at the first 6 octal digits starting from the left and expects trailing spaces or NULLs to terminate the checksum. This breaks if the checksum is right-aligned with zeros on the left, leading to a mismatch of checksums and a validation failure.

The test failure likely occurs when reading this problematic archive because `verifyCheckSum` rejects the checksum as invalid, causing the archive input stream to throw an error or not properly recognize the archive.

Next step: check if the `parseOctal` method or related places have assumptions about digit alignment, or if `verifyCheckSum` can be improved to handle zero-padded checksums on the left.

The bug can be fixed by relaxing the logic in `verifyCheckSum` to correctly parse right-aligned (left zero-padded) octal checksums or accept the trailing zeros as valid padding. Alternatively, `parseOctal` could be modified to allow such formats.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
